Lask Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Łask, Poland

Demolished. Łask, first recorded as a village in 1356 and granted town rights in 1422, saw Jewish settlement develop through 16th-century arrivals and 17th-century town privileges; population reached 77% (1,327) by 1793. By 1940, 3,366 Jews lived there, mostly Hasidim; Germans established a Judenrat under Zelman Kochman that year, followed by a ghetto (November 18, 1940) liquidated from August 23, 1942, under Hans Biebow's orders - about 70 people were murdered locally, with 900 sent to the Łódź Ghetto and 3,000 to the Chełmno extermination camp. This original cemetery, probably founded in the 18th century, was completely destroyed during WWII; Germans used its tombstones to pave about 300 meters of road in nearby Buczek. A market later occupied the site, followed by a school in the early 1960s (bodies were exhumed and transferred to Łódź's Jewish cemetery and Łask's own New Jewish Cemetery); High School No. 1 in Łask stands there today.
